chunks: "The standard I2C speeds are 100 kilohertz for Standard mode, 400 kilohertz for Fast mode, 1 megahertz for Fast-mode Plus, and 3.
4 megahertz for High-speed mode, and there's a 5 megahertz Ultra-fast mode that is write-only and push-pull.
In practice most sensors and EEPROMs run at 100 or 400 kilohertz, and newer parts support 1 megahertz. Those numbers are ceilings, not guarantees.

The limit is the physical layer: the rising edge is an RC charge through the pull-up, and the spec gives rise-time limits of 1000 nanoseconds, 300 nanoseconds and 120 nanoseconds for the first three modes.
So whether I can use 400 kilohertz depends on my pull-up and my bus capacitance. And the bus only runs as fast as the slowest device on it, plus any clock stretching.
Also, the clock rate isn't the data rate. Every byte takes nine clocks, eight bits plus the ACK, and there's an address byte and START and STOP around each transaction.
So 400 kilohertz gives at most about 44 kilobytes per second, and a short register read gets maybe half of that.
If I'm choosing, I start at 100 kilohertz because it's the most forgiving, move to 400 kilohertz when I need the throughput and the bus capacitance allows, and go to SPI if I really need megabits."
